extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of the history of advertising; historians of early modern print culture
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and exemplars of advertisements and public notices printed in mid- to late-17th-century English newspapers, showing typical content, form, and social uses (lost-property notices, nostrum ads, official proclamations, sale notices, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific physical identifiers in lost-property and animal notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements include detailed physical descriptions of lost or stolen animals and goods: breed, size, colours, distinctive marks, and damaged parts (e.g., 'less than a Grey-hound, with white under his breast', 'a httle brindled greyhound bitch, having her two hinder feet white', 'the 4th feather in one of the wings Imped, and the third pounce of the right foot broke').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show advertisers supplying exact marks and broken/unique features to enable identification ('for more particular marks'). This is presented repeatedly as the expected practice for recovery notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and locational specificity (when/where lost or sold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices supply precise timing and location details: dates like 'the eighteenth day of this instant June', places such as 'at Sittingburn or Rochester', and contexts like 'when his Majesty came thither'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly illustrates inclusion of date and place to situate the loss or event, improving chances of recovery or attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer of reward and terms of recompense
rubrics_metrics.description: Many advertisements promise a monetary reward or compensation for information or return: phrases such as 'shall be well rewarded', 'they shall have forty shillings for their pains', and 'shall have 4 times the value of the gold for his payns'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward amounts and formulas are explicitly stated to incentivise finders; advertisers sometimes promise generous or multipled recompense as a strong incentive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated contact person or place for claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads routinely instruct claimants where or to whom to report: 'leave word with Mr Samuel Merne', 'acquaint any at Whitehall', 'Mr Lambert at the Golden Key in Fleet-street'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing an explicit contact (named person, shop, or tavern) is shown as standard practice for handling returns or sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price, terms of sale, and exclusive outlets named
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial notices include pricing and precise sale arrangements: e.g., 'in sealed papers, at 12d. the paper', 'constantly to be had ... at 5 shillings a bagge', and statements of exclusive vendors 'and no others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers/authors of goods specified both cost and authorized sellers to direct buyers and to guard market control; this is used both as marketing and as an anti-counterfeit measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication and anti-counterfeit measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Sellers advertise seals, coats of arms, named booksellers, and explicit warnings: 'constantly leaveth them sealed up with his coat of arms on the papers', 'The Reader is desired to beware of counterfeits', 'This is published to prevent the designs of divers Pretenders, who counterfeit the said Lozenges'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents these devices as methods to establish provenance and protect consumers from imitation products; explicit anti-counterfeit language serves both consumer protection and the advertiser's reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand therapeutic claims and nostrum rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicinal/nostrum advertisements make broad cure claims for many diseases: 'approved for the cure of Consumption, Coughs, Catarrhs, Asthmas... and a sovereign Antidote against the Plague' and other panaceas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book remarks on the ubiquity and sometimes extravagant nature of such claims (quacks and specifics), implying an anti-pattern of overstatement; readers are warned by contemporary disclaimers about pretenders and counterfeits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of authoritative endorsement or official/political framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements and notices use royal/official authority or publisher alignment to convey legitimacy: the Mercurius Publicus was 'placed entirely under the direction of the King' and printed material like notices of the King's 'touch' for the evil; some ads and titles changed to curry favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text shows how political control or royal association influenced content and conferred perceived legitimacy (or propaganda), a factor readers should weigh when evaluating notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visual and curiosity-driven attractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers marketed illustrations and curiosities to draw crowds: 'A TRUE representation of the Rhonoserous and Elephant... engraved in Mezzotinto, printed upon a large sheet' and exhibition notices listing items like a 'choyce Egyptian Mummy, with hieroglyphicks; the Ant-Beare of Brasil; a Remora; a Torpedo; the Huge Thighbone of a Giant'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual images, engravings, and catalogues of curiosities are presented as deliberate marketing techniques to attract credulous or curious audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official public notices and procedural announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers carried formal notices for civic and trade business: e.g., 'All Artificers of the several Trades... the Committee appointed for management of that Work do sit... every Monday... there and then to treat with such as are fit to undertake the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book treats such procedural announcements as a distinct functional category of advertisement, used for coordinating rebuilding, contracts, and official business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual/circumstantial details to frame the announcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices often include the surrounding social context or circumstances (masquerades, court visits, plagues, the Great Fire) to explain why items were lost, why markets changed, or why certain products are promoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative shows advertisers leveraging current events (plague, fire, fashions) both as explanation and as marketing leverage; the presence/absence of such contextual notices is used by the author to interpret social conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertorial reflection of fashions and social habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads mirror contemporary fashions and pastimes—periwigs, hawking, lotteries, sporting animals—indicating advertisers aligned copy with prevailing tastes and amusements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book uses examples (perriwig-makers advertising for long flaxen hair, hawk notices) to show that advertisements track and shape fashion; this functions as both evidence and a criterion when studying period advertising.
